title: Pilot to profit: Banking AI needs a platform, not just a model

The institutions closing that distance are not simply adopting technology. They are building custom, compliant AI and reimagining the target operating model for an AI-first enterprise, that carries ambitious sandbox models into enterprise use. State of the union: Core challenges and differentiators. Financial institutions worldwide face macroeconomic pressure, legacy debt and a tightening regulatory net. In an era where core banking services are increasingly commoditized, intense cost pressures mean that customer experience has emerged as the primary differentiator. For Indian banks and NBFCs, the crux of the problem and the AI opportunities centre on three critical themes: transforming customer experience, combating fraud and financial crime and reaching the underserved market. Customer experience: Hyper-personalization is now the baseline. Intelligent automation is slashing servicing costs by shifting verification, document processing, and routine queries to machines redirecting human talent toward high-value advisory work. Banks can deliver the right product at the exact right moment, provided their underlying orchestration is compliant by design. Fraud and financial crime : Systemic strain is reaching a breaking point. Indian banks reported fraud amounting to ₹48,021 crore in FY26, which is a 46% year-on-year surge, despite case volumes halving as AI-enabled fraud and industrial mule networks concentrate damage into fewer, high-impact attacks. 2. Defensive AI, however, is fighting back: MuleHunter. Cognizant research puts the share of enterprises reporting moderate-to-large gaps between AI ambition and capability at 63% ⁵. In separate research across the Global 2000, two-thirds of leaders had yet to show measurable productivity gains and one in four had paused or abandoned AI deployments 6. The root cause of this stagnation is not a lack of technological capability, but a lack of enterprise readiness. Specifically, the main barriers are a lack of contextual knowledge of the enterprise, critical gaps in AI governance and trust, and limited workforce adoption. Many institutions run a few proofs of concept and confuse that excitement with scalable maturity. However, across all three core themes, an unexplainable model is an undeployable model. title: OCC’s AI Framework Leaves Borrowers Behind and Misses Key Aspects of Risk Management
excerpt: November 23, 2026. OCC’s AI Framework Leaves Borrowers Behind and Misses Key Aspects of Risk Management. By Evan LeFlore - Director of AI, Innovation, and Economic Opportunity Phillip Basil - Director of Economic Growth and Financial Stability. OCC AI Guidance Fact Sheet 11-23-26. Until this month, the federal banking agencies—the Federal Reserve (Fed), Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)—had said little publicly about the risks of AI in banking. Previously, they only released an update to their guidance regarding how banks manage the risks with their financial and statistical models, but that guidance explicitly excluded generative and agentic AI, two of the most likely and most consequential sources of AI risk. However, earlier this month the OCC went further and, on its own, released a more holistic supervisory framework for AI (AI Framework) that is intended to give its bank examiners a guide for assessing how banks are managing the risks from AI usage of all types. This is a positive move, but the AI Framework falls short in several important areas. The banking agencies are in the unique position of being able to observe all industry best practices as well as risks. As such, the purpose of such a supervisory framework, or supervisory guidance, is to provide bank examiners and the banks themselves with a set of typical “best practices” for risk management of various types of risks. Unfortunately, the OCC’s AI Framework fails to identify such best practices that would protect borrowers, appropriately assign responsibility to bank boards and senior management, and give AI risks the attention and scrutiny they require. What the AI Framework Says. The AI Framework notes at the outset that AI risk should not be considered as a separate and distinct risk category, but rather it should be treated as something that can “introduce, amplify or modify risk in existing risk categories, such as operational, compliance and credit [risks]. ” Broadly, it focuses on the consequences of AI and not technical sophistication. For example, a simple agent authorized to initiate transactions can pose more risk than a sophisticated tool that only drafts documents. The AI Framework has sixteen components, grouped into six pillars (purpose, risk, control, oversight, resilience, and assurance) that cover human review, governance, data, privacy, cybersecurity, testing, vendors, and audit. A four-tier scale sets how much scrutiny a particular case deserves, where Tier 1 includes AI characteristics that could cause the gravest consequences—“Direct action, low/no reversibility, high financial or customer impact, autonomous or partially autonomous includes autonomous payment agents and real-time credit decisioning”—and Tier 4 the least consequences. The AI Framework includes important risk management topics and aspects of risk management that are unique to the risks arising from AI. For example, the AI Framework:. Details aspects of risks from concrete hazards, from agents that move money to hallucinated fees and rates. References important AI guardrail concepts such as kill switches , circuit breakers , and rate limits. Suggests that human review and approval require “more than a nominal click,” and it flags alert fatigue when one person oversees many agents. The AI Framework also discusses customer remediation that reaches everyone affected, accountability remaining with a bank even when a third-party vendor supplies the AI, and high-speed agent activity affecting liquidity, fraud losses, and market behavior, an aspect Better Markets has emphasized before. However, the OCC’s AI Framework falls short in three key areas, discussed in the sections below. The Framework Fails to Protect Borrowers. The consequences of AI deciding who gets credit and who doesn’t are very real. For example, a recent study found that leading large language models recommend more denials and higher loan rates for Black

title: Standard Bank automates generative AI risk checks
excerpt: Standard Bank Group, a South African financial services company, has announced that it requires risk committee approval before generative AI applications reach customers or employees. It has automated much of the evidence gathering for those decisions, but the committee retains the final decision. In a technical blog post co-written by the bank and Amazon Web Services (AWS) , Amazon’s cloud computing unit, the companies compared their automated process with a traditional manual review that took roughly two weeks. They said the system generated a risk report in about two hours, a result demonstrated across six assessments. That timing excludes human review and approval. The bank had model- and change-risk reviews, but generative AI models and tools change every three to six months. It automated checks to keep those reviews current without replacing its policies. How the checks work. The assessment runs in the bank’s AWS account. An AI agent reads project documents and code, drafts answers to an initial questionnaire and links them to supporting evidence. Delivery teams check those answers and supply evidence the agent missed. The system also tests the application directly, using typical user questions, jailbreak attempts and off-topic prompts. It repeats and rephrases prompts to check whether the application’s responses remain consistent in meaning. A model on Amazon Bedrock then checks the evidence and application responses against more than 300 yes-or-no questions tied to international AI standards and the bank’s own policies. A fixed formula combines each risk’s likelihood, the proportion of missing evidence and a severity level the bank’s risk team can adjust. Findings are rated from very low to critical. Each missing piece of evidence is linked to a proposed fix and the relevant standard or policy clause. The model-based evaluations run multiple times, and conflicting risk findings are flagged for human review. Human reviewers can confirm or amend findings before the risk committee makes its decision. The software generates technical reports, a mitigation checklist and a dashboard. A separate tool turns updated internal policies into new questions, so the tests can change when the rules do. These reports support the bank’s risk decisions; they do not certify regulatory compliance. The bank has made the assessment optional during proofs of concept and mandatory during the build stage. That allows teams to identify and address gaps before seeking approval, rather than relying entirely on checks at the end of development. Six assessments, unanswered questions. After teams addressed flagged gaps, the bank reported a 14% improvement in use-case risk scores. The blog post does not provide starting scores or explain precisely how that improvement was calculated. It also does not disclose the cost of building and operating the system or how often reviewers changed the model’s findings. The assessment is already in production for use cases being prepared for launch. The bank plans to rerun checks on a schedule or after changes to code and configuration once deployed applications are connected. For now, its published results show faster report generation in six assessments, not continuous checking of deployed AI systems.

title: U.S. banks tight AI-agent controls after Hugging Face incident: Reuters
excerpt: Several large and mid-sized U. S. banks are tightening controls around their own artificial intelligence agents to prevent them from going rogue, after high-profile incidents at technology firms exposed potential weaknesses, banking and industry sources said. U. S. banks had already been blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions while also cracking down on how their own internally-developed agents function. The move to scrutinize internal agents is a reaction to experimental OpenAI models escaping testing safeguards and gaining access to systems at the ChatGPT maker, Hugging Face and other organizations, after which several banks set up internal teams to examine their systems. To avoid incidents such as those at Hugging Face, a number of U. S. banks are now limiting what internal agents within their own bank can access, for example by separating them from critical systems and improving their ability to spot and stop harmful activity, four sources familiar with the matter said. Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here. The banks are limiting how long agents can keep working, keeping passwords and records beyond their reach, and creating backup plans to keep operations running if an agent has to be shut down, one of the sources said. They are also more firmly separating agents from other technology, tightening restrictions on what they can access and bringing them within existing identity and access-management programs, two of the sources said. In addition, they are restricting the credentials given to agents, limiting the activities and systems they are authorized to access, and keeping testing environments isolated from systems used in day-to-day banking operations, according to two of the sources. The Hugging Face incident - when an OpenAI model went rogue and triggered a hack that compromised the AI startup’s infrastructure - had a chilling effect on banks’ adoption of the latest AI models, one source said, prompting tighter limits on the credentials, activities and systems available to internal agents. And while no banks have been so far affected in such incidents, several large and mid-sized banks assembled internal teams to study how the models bypassed restrictions, assess whether similar weaknesses existed in their own systems and recommend additional protections, the sources said. Latest updates on international news here. All the major U. S. banks deploy agentic AI across businesses including wealth management, payments, transactions and other corporate functions. Unlike conventional software, agents can independently make decisions, use tools and interact with multiple systems to complete a task. The banks already face challenges from having to rapidly update and fix newly discovered vulnerabilities, as easily accessible AI tools and large language models supercharge the discovery of vulnerabilities in software. JPMorgan earlier this week was hit with a software bug. Kill switches. As part of the tighter controls, banks are treating agents more like employees, with clearly defined credentials, permissions and limits, one of the sources said. Institutions also need to record which systems an agent accessed, what actions it took and whether a person approved them, the person said. Banks are more firmly separating passwords, activity records and critical security controls from AI agents, reinforcing existing safeguards intended to prevent agents from altering evidence of their actions. While some of these access controls already existed, banks have since then tested, reinforced or extended them as needed, three of the sources said. Such records allow investigators to reconstruct an incident and determine what data or systems were affected, one of the sources said. title: Bank Customers Don't Trust AI With Their Money, And Citigroup (NYSE: C), JPMorgan (NYSE: JPM), And Schwab (NYSE: SCHW) Are Counting On It
excerpt: jpmorgan bank stock. Only 49% of bank customers trust the accuracy of AI-generated financial information, compared with 79% who trust information sourced directly from bank websites, according to recent survey data. That credibility gap is proving to be a significant asset for major financial institutions as they push back against the growing ambitions of third-party AI agents seeking access to customer accounts. The conversation intensified following Meta Platforms’ (NASDAQ: META) September launch of Muse, a personal AI agent that drew widespread media attention and renewed speculation about artificial intelligence upending traditional banking. Concerns about Muse and similar tools center on scenarios where agents autonomously move money across accounts or exploit credit card reward systems at scale, potentially eroding core banking revenue streams. Yet the industry’s response has been less panic and more coordinated resistance, with several of the country’s largest financial institutions drawing clear boundaries around customer account access. Citigroup (NYSE: C), Bank of America (NYSE: BAC), and JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) have each announced they will refuse third-party AI agents or assistants permission to interact with customer accounts. Charles Schwab (NYSE: SCHW) CEO Rick Wurster struck a measured tone on the issue, telling Bloomberg last month that relatively few of the firm’s clients are even attempting to reach their accounts through unauthorized AI agents. A separate survey finding reinforces the banks’ position further, with 72% of customers expressing hesitation about sharing their financial data with generative AI tools at all. Without regulatory clarity defining the rules, liability frameworks, and permissible limits for agentic AI in financial services, banks are expected to maintain and potentially tighten those restrictions. The more telling strategic move, however, is what banks are building behind those walls, with institutions racing to develop proprietary AI products that keep customers engaged within their own ecosystems. Schwab has already unveiled an AI assistant called Charley, while JPMorgan has begun a targeted pilot of a tool named Smart Cash, designed to forecast users’ cash flow and automatically shift funds to maximize yield. By building in-house alternatives, banks are effectively using the competitive pressure from companies like Meta as a catalyst rather than a threat, channeling it into product development that strengthens customer retention. As one analyst put it plainly, “Banks are AI beneficiaries, not AI roadkill,” a framing that captures the industry’s current posture with notable precision. The emerging picture is one of an industry that has chosen to absorb and redirect technological disruption rather than cede ground to outside platforms competing for control of customer financial relationships. title: Hong Kong wants banks to use AI to catch crypto crime before money disappears
excerpt: . Back to the list Hong Kong wants banks to use AI to catch crypto crime before money disappears. coindesk. com + 1 more 18 November 2026 15:29, UTC. Hong Kong’s central bank is accelerating efforts to get banks to adopt artificial intelligence to detect financial crime as the rise of stablecoins and other digital assets makes suspicious money transfers harder to track. Raymond Chan, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's executive director for enforcement and anti-money laundering, said Tuesday the regulator is working to accelerate AI adoption among banks, including examining how AI agents could combine blockchain transactions with customer records to detect financial crime. Chan cited Chainalysis research showing illicit crypto addresses received at least $154 billion in 2025, up 162% from the previous year, largely driven by activity involving sanctioned entities, with stablecoins accounting for 84% of the total. The firm put illicit activity at less than 1% of the crypto transaction volume measured in its analysis. Banks can trace transactions on a blockchain, but identifying who controls the wallets is more difficult. “The core challenge obviously lies in linking wallet activities to real-world identities quickly enough to prevent fund dissipation,” Chan said. Abdul Rafay Gadit, co-founder of ZIG Finance, said banks should test AI agents against past fraud cases and run them alongside existing monitoring systems before allowing them to act independently. “Compare what it catches, what it misses and how long investigations take. Fewer alerts only helps if you’re still catching suspicious activity,” he said. AI agents can carry out several tasks with limited human supervision. Chan said they could flag patterns, such as rapid switches between cryptocurrencies and conventional money, that could conceal the source of funds. Identity tools to help establish who controls a wallet are also being piloted, he said. The HKMA has provided technical support and workshops to help banks deploy AI, according to a report released Tuesday by the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research. It describes one bank using generative AI to investigate possible money laundering through transaction records, images and customers' digital activity. The bank reported faster, more accurate fraud investigations without providing details. The report found 90% of surveyed financial institutions had adopted or planned to adopt generative AI. Across business use cases, 13% had implemented AI agents, and 56% planned to do so. The survey, conducted from January to March, included 39 financial institutions and eight technology providers. Banks also raised concerns about security and about how to explain AI-made decisions. Gadit said agents could gather transaction records, check sanctions lists and prepare cases for investigators, but decisions to freeze accounts, reject payments or report suspicious activity should remain with bank staff. title: US$700 Billion Opportunity: Responsible AI Could Transform Women’s Financial Inclusion, Women’s World Banking and EY Find
excerpt: TMT Newswire > GlobeNewswire. US$700 Billion Opportunity: Responsible AI Could Transform Women’s Financial Inclusion, Women’s World Banking and EY Find. by GlobeNewswire. Nov 24, 2026 10:55 am. Joint white paper examines how AI can expand credit access, enable customer-centred financial products and deliver personalised financial guidance to underserved women. Key Highlights:. Ad. Responsible AI could help financial institutions reach underserved women and unlock significant business opportunities. Three opportunities include improved credit access, customer-centred products and personalised financial guidance. Seven real-world examples demonstrate AI’s potential to advance financial inclusion. SINGAPORE, Nov. 23, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Women’s World Banking (WWB) and the EY Organization have launched The Next Billion Customers: How AI Turns Financial Inclusion into a Growth Strategy , a joint white paper examining how responsible artificial intelligence (AI) can help financial institutions identify and serve underserved women while unlocking new business opportunities. Citing the World Bank Global Findex 2025, the paper notes that approximately 700 million women lack access to a bank account. Many also lack formal credit histories or financial records, representing an estimated US$700 billion market opportunity. Angelique Timmer, Regional Head for Southeast Asia, Women’s World Banking, said, "AI presents a significant opportunity to reshape financial services so that women’s economic potential is recognised and better served. But technology alone will not deliver inclusion. AI must reflect women’s lived realities, be guided by responsible innovation and supported by partnerships. ”. The white paper identifies three areas where AI can accelerate financial inclusion: expanding credit access through improved customer assessment and lower underwriting costs; enabling financial institutions to design products around women's needs; and building trust through accessible, personalised financial guidance. It features seven examples of organisations applying AI to advance financial inclusion: AIForesee, Boost Capital, Kaleidofin, Igloo, Good With, Haqdarshak and ToumAI. Gillian Hinde, EY Global Corporate Responsibility Leader, said, "Expanding financial inclusion requires more than technology. It depends on trust, effective regulation, distribution, local knowledge, and a deep understanding of the communities these solutions are designed to serve. AI can help shape innovative solutions, but it is through global and local partnerships that we can bring inclusive finance models to the people who need them most and deliver impact at scale. ”. For financial institutions, the paper recommends positioning responsible AI governance as an enabler of growth, leveraging AI to make financial inclusion commercially viable, and building partnerships to accelerate adoption and scale. The collaboration brings together Women’s World Banking’s expertise in inclusive finance and EY’s financial services capabilities to demonstrate how responsible AI can help institutions expand access, better serve customers and build sustainable business models. About Women’s World Banking. For over 45 years, Women’s World Banking has been dedicated to serving the 700 million women excluded by the formal financial sector. We partner with financial institutions and policymakers to design, develop, and implement solutions and programs that facilitate systemic change for women. As an investor, we advance women in the workplace and as customers through direct equity to bring them security, prosperity, and independence.
